title: Looking back: the Tenth Guru's pen

lines: BEFORE SUNRISE: SHORT LINES, LIKE FOOTSTEPS.
cards: Before sunrise, in a Sikh home, someone is reading quickly. The lines are short, and they land like footsteps: no mark, no sign, no caste, no lineage. That's the Jaap Sahib, from the pen of Guru Gobind Singh.
That evening the family stands for the Ardas, and its opening lines are his too. At an amrit ceremony, his words are read over the water as it's stirred.
This year gave a whole block to his writings: praise, a life story, a letter of rebuke, a love song. Today, not a shelf of books, but a voice still heard in a Sikh's day.

teach.b: Start at dawn. The Sikh code lists the morning prayers: Guru Nanak's Japji, then two from the Tenth Guru, the Jaap Sahib and the Tav Prasad Swayye.
A morning moves from the First Guru's voice to the Tenth's, and his part is praise, name after name for the Timeless One, as if no single name were enough. Then evening.

The Rehras, the evening prayer in the code, carries his Chaupai. In paraphrase it begins: protect me with Your own hand, and let the wish of my heart be fulfilled. The warrior who wrote it asks to be held.
Then the Ardas, the prayer Sikhs say standing together.

teach.h: THE ARDAS OPENS WITH HIS STANZA.
teach.b: It opens with the first stanza of his Chandi di Var: first remember Bhagauti, the divine power, then Guru Nanak and the Gurus after him.
Bhagauti can be read as God's power, and some readers also hear the sword in that word. Either way, strength and remembrance open the shared prayer together. Then the amrit.

teach.h: THREE OF FIVE AT THE AMRIT.
teach.b: The code names five prayers read as the water is stirred with a double-edged khanda, and three are his: Jaap, the swayyas, the Chaupai.

teach.h: PEN AND STEEL, IN ONE BOWL.
teach.b: Pen and steel, in one bowl. The life story, the rebuke in the Zafarnama, the song from the wilderness are read and sung too, in katha and kirtan. Looking back, his writings aren't only admired from a distance.
They're said aloud, morning and night, in prayer, and over the water of the Khalsa.

how: Sikhs who keep the daily prayers read the Tenth Guru's Jaap Sahib and Tav Prasad Swayye in the morning and his Chaupai within the evening Rehras; the Ardas opens with his stanza from Chandi di Var.

o: a year-end look at where the Tenth Guru's lines are still heard
regret over the hard choices made in the year gone by
a prayer said for the Gurus on the last night of the year

games.why: the Ardas opens with his stanza: first remember Bhagauti, the divine power, then Guru Nanak and the Gurus after him.

practice: Here is the opening of the Jaap Sahib, in paraphrase: the One who has no mark and no sign, no caste and no lineage. Say it slowly, once, and notice: all the labels people pin on one another, and the line pins none of them on God.
If you pray, let the line be your praise; if not, let it rest in the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Looking back. Today, at the Tenth Guru's pen: his lines open the morning, fill the evening, begin the Ardas and stir the amrit. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the name of the Tenth Guru's morning hymn of praise, the Jaap Sahib.

carryVoice: Your line: pen and sword. A gentle word and a firm one, held in the same hand. Until tomorrow.
